name: Revalenta arabica

card.summary: A 19th-century patent health food sold as a lentil-based remedy, marketed as a nourishing diet for digestion and general vitality.
card.note: Historical product; contemporary analysis described it as ordinary lentil flour.

quick.overview:
Revalenta arabica was a powdered food sold in the mid-1800s as a restorative diet for a wide range of complaints. Its appeal to buyers was general health and vigour, which feeds into how a person looks and feels.

Contemporary analysis, reported by Wikipedia, found it to be a preparation of common lentil, its name derived by rearranging the older botanical name Ervum lens.
quick.how: It was sold as a meal or flour taken as a dietary staple, advertised in newspapers including colonial Australian ones in the 1850s.
quick.risks: As a lentil food, no specific harms are described in the sources; the historical issue was the breadth of its health claims.

lead: Revalenta arabica, also called Ervalenta, was a patent health food sold in the 19th century as an empirical diet for patients and advertised for conditions of the blood, brain, kidney, liver, lungs, nerves, glands and stomach.[1] Buyers used it as a general restorative aimed at vitality and wellbeing.

A mass-marketed version was identified as a preparation of common lentil whose name was formed by transposing Ervum lens; its value was compared with pea-meal.[1] An 1853 medical journal item addressed it under the title 'Revalenta Arabica quackery'.[2] The true Revalenta arabica is the root of Glossostemon bruguieri, sold as Arabgossi or moghat in Egypt and identified by Georg Schweinfurth.[1]

chain: Eaten as a daily restorative meal
angle.text: It was sold as a nourishing diet for broad health, with any appearance benefit coming through claimed better health.

paras: The product was advertised as a cure-all, including in an 1856 Hobart Courier advertisement.[1] The botanical name 'Revalenta arabica' is said to disguise Ervum lens, the lentil's older name.[1]
A medical journal item in 1853 titled 'Revalenta Arabica quackery' shows that physicians were already commenting on it.[2]
